description: Forest set aside by the community. The adherent's traditional religion of the ancestral spirits attach great respect to the environment because they argue, by despoiling it, they will be depriving their deity, Mwari, and the spirits of a home to live in. These forest patches are also important in maintaining elephant movements in this part of the Zambezi Valley. Elephants move through these forests as they travel between the Mavuradonha Mountains and the Zambezi River to the north, and they sometimes linger here, especially during the dry season when wild masawu fruit is ripe. Groups of up to ten have been seen hanging around in several forest patches.

name: Nkhotakota Wildlife Reserve
description:
Nkhotakota Wildlife Reserve is the oldest and largest reserve in all of Malawi. This 1,800 km2 reserve once contained as many as 1,500 elephants but due to decades of lawlessness and poaching the population was reduced to fewer than 100 individuals by 2015, and other key species had largely been hunted out. With most of the wildlife gone, there was no reason to visit such a quiet place; no tourism revenue was being generated and the reserve offered little employment. This large but silent forest seemed to have little to no value at all.

Upon assuming management of Nkhotakota in 2015 in partnership with the Department of National Parks and Wildlife (DNPW), African Parks immediately began preparing for what would become one of the world’s largest wildlife translocations, to breathe life back into this place. By August 2017, over a two-year period, the park received over 500 elephants and 2,000 other animals from two other parks in Malawi.

With Nkhotakota’s wildlife restored, tourism is now flourishing with visitors coming from near and far to spot the reserve’s herd of almost 600 elephants. With an increase in visitors, employment has increased, school scholarships are being funded, and livelihood projects are running. It is still early days for this vast reserve but in just a few short years, Nkhotakota is now developing along a pathway of hope and possibility, where for the first time in decades, local communities are beginning to experience the benefits of this newly-revived reserve.

name: Irregele Milato
description:
The Irregele Milato planting site comprises 756 hectares in the Quelimane District of Zambezia Province, where today, local people often rely on fishing, agriculture and charcoal production for their livelihoods. The necessity for timber for income and for use in daily life has led to extensive deforestation in the area, and flooding in these deforested areas also causes further damage to the ecosystem and to people’s homes and property.

Mangroves are a small, coastal tree species that occur worldwide in the tropics and subtropics, and are particularly proficient at absorbing carbon and storing it in their extensive root systems underground. Carbon stored in mangrove forests is considered blue carbon, because it is stored on the coast. In addition to their excellent carbon sequestration abilities, mangroves provide excellent flood and storm protection to the coastal area itself.

Throughout the project period, our community will fund a projected 6 million mangrove trees in this planting site, which will help to stabilise the soil, absorb carbon, and provide employment to local planters and forest guards.

name: Musengezi Forest
description: The forest is protected by traditional authority as a sacred forest as home to the ancestral spirits. The site is alluvial woodland in an oxbow of the Musengezi river 6 km north of Musengezi Mission. The vegetation is dense forest with a thick shrub layer, particularly at the margins, situated on a light but clay-rich alluvium of some age. The major trees, large and mostly over-mature, are Kigelia africana, Trichilia emetica, Cordyla africana, Ficus sycomorus, Garcinia livingstonei and Diospyros mespiliformis. Smaller trees and shrubs include Drypetes mossambicensis, Cordia goetzei, Antidesma venosum, Dalbergia arbutifolia, Oncoba spinosa, Phyllanthus reticulatus, Cleistochlamys kirkii, Deinbollia xanthocarpa and Lecaniodiscus fraxinifolius.

name: Degraded Forest Restoration-Adopt A Tree Project
description:
Objective
This project aims to increase local tree planting to ensure future environmental conservation is guaranteed around seven catchment areas within Gembe Hills, Mbita Constituency, Homabay County, Kenya. That is based on achieving the following aims: 
•	To empower communities and the youth to create a safer, healthier, cleaner, and greener environment. 
•	To alleviate poverty by building, strengthening, and empowering communities to produce adequate food without destroying the environment.
This concept note does a great job summarizing the program highlighting the importance of the project to bring environmental sustainability, and focusing on the activities and output of the project. 
Project Themes: Tree planting for households and community empowerment – people’s empowerment drive.
Project Description
The project will be implemented in Gembe Hills, Homa Bay County, to demonstrate climate change mitigation measures using tree planting in establishing agroforestry as part of increasing community-based support for the development of measures put in place to mitigate environmental and climatic change around the selected location. The project will involve communities to achieve and strengthen sustainable farming and climate change adaptation. 
The primary focus of this project is the communities. The Gembe Hills site comprises 2,709 hectares near Lake Victoria in Nyanza, Kenya. This site is close to Mount Homa, also known as Got Marahuma or God Uma in the Luo language, and Ruma National Park, which is home to Jackson's hartebeest, roan antelopes, and reticulated giraffes. This site lies within Homa Bay County and near the town of the same name, which has 45,000 people.
The predominant ethnic group near Gembe Hills is the Suba people. The Suba is a diverse Kenyan Bantu who traditionally relies on small-scale agriculture and livestock raising. These communities raise cattle and grow crops such as cassava, sorghum, potatoes, and maize. Unfortunately, increased human expansion into surrounding forests, combined with a lack of forest management, have resulted in reliance on the forest for firewood and charcoal production, both for commercial and subsistence use. This charcoal dependency has depleted much of the forest stock.
The project will implement its proven One Person-One Tree methodology and inspire and engage the community members to reforest their terrestrial ecosystems through the planting of 50,000 trees by May 2023, which is the first phase of the tree planting project. The team aims to restore their environment while lifting local communities from extreme poverty.

This site is a shared site supervised by Eden Reforestation Projects. 

The channel is near Lamu Town, a UNESCO World Cultural Heritage site that has an incredibly rich history. The surrounding areas (including this project site) have a history of trade with countries as far away as India, dating back to the 12th century. The local artisans still make dhows (traditional sailing vessels) by hand.

Historically, mangroves have been an important part of the local economy. They were harvested for dhow construction, export for the tanning industry (ash and bark), and building materials. Mangrove harvesting was banned in 1997, but harvesting continued despite the ban. Recently, legal harvesting has been reinstated (as of 2019). name: Kijabe, Lari
description:
This is a shared site supervised by Eden Reforestation Projects. 

The cultural and ecological heritage of Kenya’s forests is vibrant and unique, but in recent decades the country has been battling soil erosion more intensely as a result of unsustainable practices. 

Rural communities work closely with the Kijabe city council, the local forest trust and surrounding agricultural and pastoral communities on reforesting the area. Localized knowledge on biodiverse habitats and strong ties to authorities ensure that forests can be fully restored on the outskirts of Kijabe, an old town famous for its strict conduct. The sale of alcohol, cigarettes or condoms remain forbidden to this day – a remaining legacy of missionaries arriving in 1903. 

This forest is also an important home and corridor for wildlife. Animals use this area to move between the dry floor of the Rift Valley and the protected, lush forests of the Kenyan highlands. On such terrain, olive trees are a great way to ensure erosion control. Their extensive root system grips the ground, reducing the process of wind and water erosion. 

As local families from Kijabe plant these trees, the resident community receives sustainable employment opportunities, a reliable water supply and landslide protection amongst many other benefits.

name: Nashulai Maasai Conservancy
description:
Nashulai's interdependent mission: Conserve Wildlife–Preserve Culture–Reverse Poverty. In 2016, facing dire poverty and biodiversity collapse, we rallied to save our land and community by creating the first indigenous community owned/run conservancy in East Africa. To regenerate our land and culture; we promote the inclusion for our people in the Kenyan economy from which many had been excluded through sustainable social enterprises, ensuring they get economic benefits, not costs, for sharing their land with our wildlife; and invite collaboration with other indigenous and scientific communities. Promoting gender equality through education, economic empowerment, and advocacy, is another important dimension. 

A 2020 UNDP Equator Prize winner, Nashulai accomplished much in its 4 years. Tearing down 25km of fencing we restored 5,000 acres of grassland in a critical migration corridor. We’re a member in good standing with Kenya Wildlife Conservancies Association (KWCA) and the Maasai Mara Wildlife Conservancies Association (MMWCA),built 2 new schools, launched our Cultural Training Institute, and educated thousands on women’s rights. During the 4 month Covid-19 lockdown we fed over 28,000 weekly in villages 100km away, created social enterprises for community economic empowerment, and mobilized community anti-poaching patrols.

Over 30 years our land became heavily deforested due to land use changes and illegal logging, especially along the Sekenani River, upstream of the Mara River. The Sekenani River has become heavily eroded, with lowered water levels, increased flash floods and drying up during droughts. Part of the Mara River Basin, this has contributed to the degradation of the globally significant Mara River, which is predicted to dry up in 3-8 years without immediate action. Reforestation will be critical to restoring the Sekenani River and Mara River Basin’s health. In addition to this, Nashulai is a critical connecting wildlife corridor allowing the Great Migration to pass safely through our land from the Maasai Mara National Reserve to other conservancies to the east, as well as providing safe habitat for many other species, including threatened, endangered, and critically endangered species. In addition to the ecological and wildlife benefits of reforesting the area, there are also marked benefits to local Maasai communities, including improved health through improved water quality and access to traditional medicinal plants, decreased impacts of droughts on community and livestock, increased access to alternative and sustainable forms of income, and protection of the Maasai way of life.

Since our founding, we have been working to restore our land which had been heavily deforested due to illegal logging and firewood harvesting. We started our reforestation efforts by removing fences to support wildlife-assisted seed dispersal, introducing our rangers/scouts to prevent illegal logging, and working with communities to prevent over-harvesting. While we planted 1,000s of seed balls and over 100s of saplings throughout Nashulai in the first four years, our biggest reforestation activity to date is the Sekenani River Restoration Project. This May, more than 700 community members planted 25,000 seed balls of various acacia species, and 4,000 indigenous tree saplings along the Sekenani River and springs within our conservancy. Reforestation efforts on a larger scale are also supported by including reforestation in our publicly available conservation courses at our Cultural Training Centre and in the training/support we have provided for two newly created conservancies. We have also initiated our own plant nursery which we plan to use to expand our reforestation efforts both within Nashulai and in other communities.

name: Dundori Forest phase 1a
description:
Dundori Forest, in Nakuru County (about 200km North-West of Nairobi), is a Key Biodiversity Area, signifying its species and habitat importance and associated conservation efforts. The waters within this Key Biodiversity Area feed into the three major lakes in Kenya (one being a UNESCO World heritage site), making it vital for water security. Dundori Forest is part of the six western forest blocks of Nakuru County and plays a critical role in regional biodiversity conservation and ecosystem services, being part of the larger Mau water tower.

The objective of this project is to restore 200 hectares of highly degraded forests through sustainable, community-led reforestation. The project specifically seeks to catalyse the rehabilitation and restoration of watershed functions, soil stability and quality, carbon sequestration and the biodiversity of the degraded Dundori forest by replanting local species and engaging local communities in their efforts to restore and protect the forest. Additionally, the project will involve planting of trees in schools, as a means to engage young environmental stewards in forest and school-based tree growing in 15 learning institutions.

name: AGROFOREST MONAPO
description:
The consequences of deforestation, also widespread in the country, include frequent floods and landslides, soil erosion, and silting of reservoirs, causing serious ecological and environmental problems and complex feedback effects on agricultural production along the Monapo River basin. Faced with massive environmental degradation, given the need to mitigate climate change and the increased demand for firewood, fodder, and wood, agroforestry practices systems are promising and may be the solution to the problem. The Monapo region has been cultivated for a long time and moderate to severe soil erosion is occurring. Deforestation/soil erosion has been a problem, with a number of associated economic and environmental implications, particularly along major access roads. It is estimated that, in the medium and long term, the District may suffer from soil impoverishment and desertification.
Changes in land use and intensification of agriculture affect the biodiversity of managed landscapes. In light of ongoing environmental degradation, there is growing consensus that integrated tree crop production systems, such as agroforestry, are the way to manage tropical agroecosystems in general and fragile ecosystems in particular.
In addition, agroforestry, which aims to optimize productivity and, above all, sustainability, has the potential to provide many resources on which peoples traditionally depended on forests (fuel, fodder, green manure, and wood).

name: Kenya Schools Botanic Gardens Initiative
description:
In response to this pressing issue of Climate Change, Saving-Planet envisions a transformative project that transcends the boundaries of traditional education. Our goal is to establish one-hectare botanic gardens within the premises of each participating school, with a focus on nurturing native tree species endemic to the respective regions.With Kenya boasting a total of 37,930 primary and secondary schools, this nationwide project will create a profound impact on the environment, education, and local communities. Our vision is to plant 60,688,000 indigenous trees across these gardens, covering a staggering 37,930 hectares of land. This initiative aligns with the broader national effort to increase forest cover while simultaneously improving the livelihoods of local communities.
 The botanic gardens are not just green spaces; but they are living museums, educational centers, and research hubs. By creating one-hectare botanic gardens, we aim to achieve several interrelated objectives:
 Biodiversity Conservation: Native tree species are the backbone of any ecosystem. By nurturing these species, we contribute to the preservation of Kenyan biodiversity. These gardens will serve as sanctuaries for endangered plant species while facilitating research on conservation techniques.
 Education: Our schools will become living classrooms where students can engage with their natural environment. They will learn about the importance of trees, ecology, and sustainable land management. This hands-on education will create a generation of environmentally conscious citizens.
 Climate Resilience: Native trees have adapted to local environmental conditions over generations. By growing these species, we enhance the resilience of local ecosystems to climate change, desertification, and drought conditions. This, in turn, benefits local communities by protecting their livelihoods.
 Community Engagement: We view this project as a collaborative effort involving students, teachers, parents, and the wider community. By actively participating in the establishment and maintenance of these gardens, community members will gain a sense of ownership and pride in their local environment.
 Our school tree planting project is not merely a response to Kenya's low forest cover; it is a declaration of our commitment to a sustainable and prosperous future. By cultivating one-hectare botanic gardens, we are sowing the seeds of knowledge, environmental stewardship, and resilience in the hearts and minds of our students and communities. Together, we aim to restore Kenya's forests, protect its biodiversity, and secure a brighter tomorrow for all.
WHY THIS SITE?
Kenya's schools offer ample unused land, a valuable resource for reforestation. This strategy not only restores native trees but also educates the youth, instilling a sense of conservation, and enhances school landscapes with indigenous greenery.
LONG TERM PROTECTION
Planting 60,688,000 indigenous trees in 38,000 hectares of botanic gardens.-Transforming schools into hubs for ecological education.-Fostering an appreciation for nature and sustainable practices.-Empowering Kenya's youth to contribute to a healthier, more sustainable society.

name: Just Digg It Project
description:
As our satellites pass over regions of Kenya and Tanzania, they are capturing a tremendous transformation happening on the ground. Land that has been dry and parched for years is now sprouting green grasses and young trees. Rainwater is reviving the land and supporting restored and thriving African native ecosystems. This metamorphosis is the impact of collaborative efforts between local pastoral communities and Justdiggit, a nonprofit dedicated to supporting land restoration through nature-based solutions. And using our satellite data, including SkySat, PlanetScope, and Planetary Variables, Justdiggit quantifies, evaluates, and scales these transformative projects with tangible metrics.

Aptly named, Justdiggit supports local farmers and pastoralists in Tanzania and Kenya to use accessible tools, like shovels, to dig bunds—semi-circular shaped pits that help the soil capture rainwater. In regions impacted by drought and loss of natural vegetation, the top layer of soil can harden and act as a seal, but by digging through the dry layer, rain water can trickle down and hydrate the parched land. This ancient regenerative practice cools down the temperature of the region by allowing native grasses and trees to grow back, and this landscape change can be captured by Planet’s satellite imagery. Justdiggit uses mobile technology, data, and communication to scale up their impact on the African continent and to create awareness around nature-based solutions world-wide.

name: Njoro Sub-County
description: The Planet cooler restorers projects aims to restore the landscape in Njoro Sub County through planting of 5 million trees by the year 2030. The project will mainly plant fruit trees, Grevillea Robusta trees, and indigenous tree species. This will enhance the tree cover in the target area by 30%. The trees will be planted through an agro forestry approach in private farms within the location. To enable this, the planet coolers restorers’ project will produce tree seedlings at its nursery site at Gachuhi center. These seedlings will then be issued to farmers to plant on their farms. Proper preparation of the planting areas will have to be done before the seedlings are issued to ensure that issued seedlings are actually planted properly. Farmers will be assisted with the site preparation work. Also, the farmers will be sensitized and capacity built to improve their knowledge and skills on agro forestry and restoration in general. The project area was chosen because of the wanton degradation that has occurred over the years. This degradation has had negative effects on the community’s livelihoods making them very vulnerable, especially to the impacts of climate change. This has mainly manifested through soil degradation leading to sharp drops in agricultural production and which had multiplier negative effects on the area socioeconomic wellbeing. The degradation also had many negative ecological impacts including reduction in stream flows of rivers such as River Nderit, River Naishi, and River Njoro. These rivers were important sources of water to the community. The rivers also feed the Nakuru National park, which has an alkaline lake. They are thus the source of drinking water to the wildlife in the national park. The area is thus also the catchment area for Lake Nakuru which is a very important biodiversity hotspot that is particularly highly famous for the large populations of flamingos that it supports. The project thus aims to restore the local forest landscape through agro forestry for improvement of biodiversity, ecosystem services and building of community resilience to climate change. This will be achieved through agro forestry tree planting, sensitization and capacity building, and livelihoods improvement through restoration work. Besides, the project will improve support community based natural resources management strategies, improve food security, engage in advocacy for landscape restoration, improve environmental governance, create job and business opportunities through agroforestry, improve water quality and availability for human and wildlife use among other benefits.

description:
This coastal area contains mangrove forests that harbor a diverse array of mangrove trees and other related tree species. Also, a variety of plants and animals thrive in this area. One of the primary initiatives undertaken by ZAVECO involves raising awareness about the critical importance of mangroves. 

ZAVECO has been working together with the coastal communities to restore and conserve these areas by creating awareness on the importance of mangroves and organising fieldtrips the organization orchestrates field trips during which students and volunteers join forces with local community members. Together, they engage in activities such as harvesting local seeds and planting both mangrove tree seeds and seedlings.

Beyond these conservation endeavors, ZAVECO is committed to addressing the root causes of environmental degradation in the area. Recognizing the pressures faced by coastal communities, the organization invests in creating alternative livelihoods, like bee-keeping and sustainable aquaculture. name: Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation initiative
description:
Rusinga Island has been a very productive site experiencing heavy rainfall that has been very beneficial to farmers within the island, hence the establishment of communities. As the population grew in the 20th and 21st centuries, destruction of indigenous trees by men and women who depend on firewood for their livelihood has buried the dream of a forested environment for the community at large. The sustainable way of dealing with nature, anchored in the original culture and consciousness of the native population – among other things through taboos – had been lost. The island is now classified as a semi-arid region, although in the past it was a forested area with good climatic conditions that supported the growth of crops and also wildlife habitat. Actually there's a need of mitigating Climate Change in the region and this is the main reason as to why "A Million+ Tree Campaign Project" was initiated . Regenerating our mother earth for our future generations is all that we wish. 
Our main target is to educate, plant and grow 1 million trees and above targeting production of seedlings and distributing in schools, hospitals, churches, market as well as considering the natural ecosystems: hills, forest etc. We have tried also to introduce strategic and environmental governance expectations and enforcement of the Forestry Act of 2005  to community members to ensure investments in the project are managed 'by the people, for the people. On the other hand, we has also taken the situation into account and is striving to increase Kenya’s forest cover to the internationally required standard of over 10% trees on total land area so as to Influence the rainfall patterns in the area and increase crop yield, Create the traditional live (tree) hedges that originally surrounded Luo homesteads to increase forest cover in the area, Create the traditional live (tree) hedges to act as security fencing, protect from intruders, and provide fruit for consumption and income-generation, Create the traditional live (tree) hedges to provide dry twigs and branches for use for cooking, as was done traditionally, and so discourage felling of tress for firewood.

name: Lake Kivu Shores and the Vicinity of Volcanoes National Park
description:
Rwanda’s ecosystems lie within and are characteristic of a larger ecological and geographical region or ecoregion of East Africa called the Albertine Rift. Due in part to its location within the biodiversity-rich Albertine Rift and because of its varied landscapes and climates, Rwanda is one of Africa’s most important biodiversity areas (REMA, 2010a). Its landscape is made up of a variety of ecosystems, including humid Afromontane forests, planted forests and remnant forests such as riparian gallery forests; savannahs; a large network of water bodies (lakes, rivers and wetlands); and large cropland and grazing areas (REMA,2009).
Lake Kivu basin is among the most fragile and highly sensitive ecosystems in the region. The lake is being affected by atmospheric pollution, sedimentary, anthropogenic and climate change threats (Bootsma et al., 1999; Hecky et al., 2006). In the southern part of the Lake the demographic pressure and associated anthropogenic activities coupled with the micro-catchment topography contribute to increased degradation of land and water resources. The excessive growth of human populations in the Lake Kivu basin, land use, urbanisation, deforestation, intensive agriculture and climate warming prompt changes in the water quality of the lake. The major sources of nitrogen and phosphorus appears to be rivers and the atmosphere. The increase in sediment and nutrients loading pose a threat to biodiversity. The Lake Kivu basin is undergoing severe habitat fragmentation and deforestation. Settlements and agriculture fields in the watersheds are made available at the cost of clearing forests that also has survival impacts on lake and river systems. Deforestation and soil degradation in the upper parts of the Lake Kivu watersheds are reducing agricultural productivity and negatively affecting farmers’ livelihoods. The basin is exposed to severe overall mean soil erosion risk of 30 t/ha/yr due to both natural factors (abundant tropical precipitation and steep slopes) and anthropogenic activities without prior appropriate conservation practices.
Sebeya -Nile divide. Sebeya is a Level 2 catchment and part of the larger Level 1 Lake Kivu catchment. Sebeya catchment has a total surface area of 336.4 km², approximately 1.4 % of the total surface area of Rwanda (26,338 km²) and includes four Districts: Rubavu, Rutsiro, Ngororero and Nyabihu. The main river in the catchment is the Sebeya River, which flows for 48 km, running in a north-westerly direction from its origin in the mountains (2,660 masl) to its outflow into Lake Kivu at the town of Rubavu (1,470 masl) (MoE, 2018).
Established in 1925, Volcanoes National Park is one of the Rwandan PA with 160.3 km2 in size and situated in the northwest part of Rwanda. It protects a rich mosaic of montane ecosystems that form part of the Virunga Massif and are home to the critically endangered Mountain Gorilla. Located on the borders with Uganda and the Democratic Republic of Congo it is a member of the Greater Virunga Transboundary Collaboration, ratified by international treaty in 2015. It was also designated as a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve in 1983.

name: Introduction of agroforestry practices to mitigate climate change in the Lifidzi watershed in Tete
description:
Climate change is the most serious environmental threats facing the world today. Global warming, due to the increase of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases in the atmosphere is becoming manifest day by day. Agroforestry is an alluring option for sequestering CO2 on agricultural lands as it can sequester significant amounts of CO2 while leaving the bulk of the land in agricultural production. Basically there are three mechanisms involved through which agroforestry can help reduce atmospheric CO2 levels (Montagnini and Nair, 2004), viz., i) carbon sequestration (creating new stocks in growing trees and soil), ii) carbon conservation (eases anthropogenic pressure on existing stocks of C in forests through conservation and management efforts) and iii) carbon substitution (substitution of energy demand materials by renewable natural resources, fuel wood production, increased conversion of biomass into durable wood products for use in place of energy intensive materials). Perennial systems like home gardens and agro forests can store and conserve considerable amounts of CO2 in living biomass and also in processed wood products. However, agroforestry remains under-recognized as a greenhouse gas mitigation option for agriculture. 

Modern agriculture used on a large scale by producers around the world is in conflict with current environmental issues. Today, there are several discussions about the growing invasion of agriculture in areas of great environmental relevance. However, the food market is essential to guarantee the quality of life of populations, so it is necessary to find new forms of sustainable production. The use of Agroforestry Systems (SAFs) is an alternative form of production, which seeks to reconcile traditional agriculture with forest species.
Current agricultural activity in the Lifidzi River basin region is characterized by low productivity, as a result of the lack of incentive to production and soil degradation due to inadequate management, which generates, among other consequences, erosion and a decrease in the content of organic matter. in soils, rural poverty and rural exodus.
One of the factors that strongly influences this situation is the presence in the region of large areas cultivated in an unsustainable way, that is, practicing traditional agriculture that consists of cutting and burning the fields and mainly by the deforestation of the sources of the rivers that make up the river basin. Lifidzi, in large numbers by vegetable producers who prefer to produce on the banks of rivers because they are more fertile and are also close to water sources to facilitate the rudimentary irrigation that is common within the region.
Before starting the design of this project, a technical visit was carried out in the region of the Lifidzi River basin, both to recognize the location and to analyze the feasibility of implementing an Agroforestry System in the area. During this visit, the possibility of implementing the SAF was attested, not only in terms of the favorable local conditions, but also in the interest of the current demands of world agricultural practices in which Mozambique subscribed.

name: Lake Elementaita Restoration Site
description:
Lake Elementaita is a shallow alkaline lake lying on the Rift Valley floor in Kenya. It is fed by inflows from the rivers Mbaruk, Kariandusi, Kikopey,Chamuka and Mereroni. The key values provided by Lake Elementaita are globally significant biodiversity. It is globally recognized as an Important Bird Area due to the assemblage of various birds of conservation concern such as the threatened, range-restricted Grey-crested Helmet-shrike (Near threatened) which occurs in the surrounding woodland where it may be resident. Other birds in this area include Lesser Flamingo (Near threatened), Jackson’s Widowbird (Near threatened), African Crowned Eagle (Near threatened), Greater Spotted Eagle (Vulnerable), Martial Eagle (Vulnerable) and Whiteheaded Vulture (Vulnerable).It also sustains significant populations of over 100 species of Palearctic migratory birds by offering a vital wintering ground for them making this one of the greatest ornithological spectacles on earth. In addition, the lake supports one of the major breeding colonies of the Great White Pelicans in the world and forms part of the Great Rift Valley migratory flyway system for migratory birds. Lake Elementaita was designated an Important Bird Area in 1999 by Birdlife International and a Ramsar Site in 2005 by the Ramsar Convention Secretariat. It was named a World Heritage Site in 2011 by Unesco World Heritage Centre.
Numerous human activities within and around the lake threaten the unique and fragile balance of the lake causing a serious threat to biodiversity. These anthropogenic activities include clearing of natural vegetation for charcoal and firewood, urbanization and intensive river water abstraction for farming and commercial mining of salt for livestock. Domestic waste from mushrooming hotels and lodges around the lake is also adding to the pollution of this important wetland. Poor agricultural practices by small scale farmers in the upper catchment, most of which is by subsistence farmers is also a major threat to the lake. Unsustainable farming practices have led to siltation of streams and rivers in the headwaters and the lake. Furthermore, the eastern shores of the lake have been settled by a rapidly increasing population of subsistence farmers. Urbanization and infrastructure development and other types of development causing land use change are also a major threat to the lake. For instance, the ongoing construction of a big city along Mbaruk River which feeds the lake is likely to have adverse effects on the water supply to the lake. The Construction of this city without adequate mitigation measures, threatens the biophysical environment.
The Unfinished Agenda Africa therefore proposes a project for the restoration of Lake Elementaita ecosystem. The proposed project area is highly prone to erosion due to steep gradients compounded by poor land use practices and therefore is a key area for reducing land degradation. Within this context, the key environmental problem to be addressed by the project is land degradation, water pollution and loss of biodiversity. The project objective is to restore forest ecosystem and reduce land degradation in Lake Elementaita catchment area for increased protection of Lake Elementaita’s water resources, biodiversity, and associated ecosystem services. The high-level theory of change of the proposed project is that if the local community is supported to implement landscape restoration, overall threats to the Lake Elementaita and its associated ecosystem services will be reduced. The project will give priority to forest land management and restoration interventions in the upper catchment area of the lake for enhanced water and biodiversity protection. The project will also support smallholder farmers through training and facilitation to adopt best farming practices that enhance soil and water conservation measures and restore the lake's ecosystem.

The bay is characterized by its intricate network of wetlands, islands, and submerged vegetation, creating a dynamic habitat crucial for numerous aquatic organisms.
Masisori Swamps, nestled within the vicinity of Mara Bay, further contribute to the ecological richness of the KBA. These swamps play a pivotal role in regulating water quality, supporting biodiversity, and providing essential breeding grounds for various species. The wetlands in this KBA serve as crucial sites for migratory birds and it is recognized as Important Bird Area (IBA) by Birds Life International, adding to the area's biodiversity significance.
The bay provides critical breeding and feeding grounds for Critical Endangered species of Labeo Victorianus, Freshwater Decapods, Freshwater Odonates and Freshwater Molluscs  which face increasing threats in the region.

name: Ok Kinyei Conservancy
description:
Ol Kinyei, pioneering conservation models in the Mara ecosystem

Ol Kinyei Conservancy in Kenya is the first in the Mara ecosystem where an area of over 8,000 acres was set aside by the community for wildlife and without the presence of human settlements and cattle. Ol Kineyei achieved IUCN Green List status in 2018 for its good governance, sound design and planning, and effective management.

The conservancy is now 17,500 acres and belongs to a Maasai community who set aside the land for the purposes of wildlife conservation providing them with tangible returns to help them improve their lives and not be solely dependent on cattle. The Conservancy was formed in 2005 through a partnership between 171 local private landowners and Gamewatchers Safaris & Porini Safari Camps.

The camp is operated with the objective of creating income for the community through employment and the leasing of land. The landowners are paid per acre of leased land as well as a fee per bed-night occupied, and 90% of the camp’s staff comes from the community.

The Area

Located within the Serengeti-Mara ecosystem, Ol Kinyei is renowned for its unspoilt and breath-taking scenery with diverse terrain offering open savannah plains on one hand and rolling hills on the other. The land, with its abundance of water sources in the form of springs, streams and rivers, coupled with spectacular views across the Mara plains, is home to a wide variety of animal species.

Since the formation of the Conservancy, many indigenous species have returned to the land. The Conservancy is now home to a wide variety of wildlife including a resident pride of over 30 lions. Several leopards also have their territories within the conservancy and are often sighted by guests. Cheetahs are frequently seen and it is not rare to come across large numbers of giraffes as well as Cape buffalo and elephants. There are also over 300 species of bird. In addition, the wildebeest migration passes through Ol Kinyei when herds from the eastern plains of Loita join the migration to the Mara Reserve.

Governance

The Ol Kinyei Group Ranch was one of the traditional grazing areas for the Maasai, north of Mara National Reserve. In the early 1990s, the Group Ranch leaders embarked on the subdivision of their lands to the north of the Maasai Mara National Reserve. Most of the sections of the Ranches were subdivided into plots ranging from 60 to 150 acres. With the fragmentation of the Group Ranches, the wildlife dispersal areas surrounding the Maasai Mara National Reserve became increasingly threatened, as the rangeland was rapidly being converted into agricultural smallholdings and community settlements.

In 2005, the Ol Kinyei Conservancy partnered with landowners and tourism operators, equally participating in the Conservancy management. Their collaboration aimed to establish an area of protected wildlife habitat and allow the regeneration of vegetation, and to increase the wildlife populations so that eco-tourism could be undertaken and income generated for the local community through land leases and employment. This partnership has created a stable platform for conservation and has ensured a fair distribution of the benefits derived from conservation amongst its landowner community members, developing a greater sense of ownership, appreciation and understanding of the importance of conserving Kenya’s wildlife heritage.

Ol Kinyei Conservancy was the first conservancy to be established in the Maasai Mara Ecosystem along this model, with approximately 5,000 acres of private land leased to Porini Ol Kinyei Ltd on a 5-year initial lease. The conservancy lies between the Maasai Mara National Reserve and the Loita Plains, directly in the wildlife dispersal zone and critical habitat for the Loita wildebeest migration. It comprises open savannah plains, riverine forest, springs, streams and rivers, rolling hills and spectacular views across the Mara.

Since 2005, the conservancy has steadily grown and is currently 18,500 acres and now has one of the highest densities of lions. The cheetah population has grown steadily and the conservancy now has several families and many young cubs. The conservancy is also listed as one of the critical ecological connectivity corridor for elephants. A 2016 study on elephant movement documents Ol Kinyei Conservancy as one of the critical pathways for elephant dispersal and feeding.

name: Ufipa Plateau
description:
Ufipa plateau is the second largest and most populous zone in Rukwa region at Sumbawanga District. It is most important agro-ecological zone and half of the population obtain livelihood but also as a large part of surplus agricultural production comes in this zone. The plateau is lying between two wings of rift valley formed by Lake Tanganyika and Lake Rukwa. The natural vegetation on most of the plateau is miombo woodland. This zone covers almost 150,000 ha and contains about half of the region’s population. The residents of the area are fipa tribes (Wafipa) who involves in subsistence farming as their economic activities of raising crops such as maize, beans, cassava, groundnuts, finger millets and cattle keeping.
Ufipa plateau is facing rapid deforestation and degradation of land resources. Population growth and concentration of people have resulted in extensive forest clearing for agricultural use, overgrazing, and exploitation of existing forests for fuel wood, fodder, and construction materials. Agriculture is generally acknowledged as the main driver of deforestation where forests are cleared to make space for crops or cattle farms. The deforestation is resulting to massive environmental degradation and constituting a serious threat to sustainable agriculture, forestry and green growth development.
To counteract this situation Life Change Rukwa Development Organization (LCRDO) is proposing most ambitious programme of restoration of forest landscape and conservation of Ufipa plateau within the 3 years. Also LCRDO recognizes that planting trees is one of the biggest and cheapest ways of taking CO2 out of the atmosphere to tackle the climate crisis. Not only do forests act as carbon sinks, but they also provide vital habitat for animals and ecological services for humans, such as purifying the air we breathe and regulating local temperatures.
Responsible reforestation programs can stabilize land from erosion or natural disasters, improve soil health and groundwater recharge, promote native and endemic fauna, and provide economic development for nearby communities.

Unfortunately, Lake Olbolosat is currently facing a major issue of drying up due to the effects of climate change. The lake, which was once a major source of water for the local communities and wildlife, has drastically reduced in size over the years. The once vibrant shoreline has now turned into a dusty wasteland, with many species of plants and animals disappearing due to the lack of water. 

This alarming situation has been caused by a combination of factors such as rising temperatures, prolonged droughts, and increased evaporation. These factors have all been exacerbated by human activities such as deforestation, overgrazing, and pollution. As a result, the lake is now at a critical point where urgent action needs to be taken to restore it to its former state. 

We strongly believe that reforestation is one of the most effective solutions to help revive the biodiversity of drying Lake Olbolosat. By planting trees and other vegetation on the land beside the lake, we can help combat climate change by absorbing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and reducing temperature levels. Not only will this help in preserving the lake, but it will also provide a natural habitat for wildlife and improve the overall biodiversity of the area.

name: Zambian Southern Miombo woodlands ecoregion
description:
The Zambian Southern Miombo woodlands are a tapestry of towering miombo trees, vibrant grasslands, and meandering waterways. This ecoregion brims with a wealth of plant and animal life, from majestic elephants and elusive leopards to flitting bee-eaters and industrious termites. However, beneath this beauty lies a realm beset by numerous challenges threatening its future.

1. Deforestation: The most pressing threat is undoubtedly deforestation. Driven by the expansion of agriculture, charcoal production, and unsustainable logging practices, trees are vanishing at an alarming rate. This not only decimates habitat but also disrupts crucial ecological processes, impacting biodiversity and climate regulation.

2. Poaching and Wildlife Depletion: The allure of bushmeat and valuable animal parts fuels illegal poaching, jeopardizing the populations of iconic species like elephants, rhinos, and pangolins. This depletion disrupts predator-prey dynamics and weakens the delicate web of life within the ecosystem.

3. Climate Change: The ever-worsening grip of climate change poses a significant threat. Erratic rainfall patterns, prolonged droughts, and rising temperatures exacerbate existing problems like bushfires and habitat loss, pushing the woodlands towards further vulnerability.

4. Poverty and Livelihoods: The poverty that grips many local communities living in the miombo woodlands creates a complex dynamic. Dependence on land-based resources for survival often leads to unsustainable practices, unintentionally contributing to the challenges the ecosystem faces.

5. Limited Conservation Resources: Underfunded conservation efforts and a lack of awareness about the importance of the miombo woodlands further hinder effective protection measures. The gap between the scale of the threats and the resources available to combat them is undeniably daunting.

Furthermore, it plays a pivotal role in the socio-economic development of the region by facilitating large-scale rice production and hydro-electrical power generation.

Similar to numerous other river systems, this catchment confronts severe and ongoing degradation stemming from factors such as climate change, shifts in land use, and inadequate institutional management. Immediate action is imperative to address these challenges, necessitating the implementation of conservation initiatives and water management strategies. These endeavors should encompass measures to safeguard the river's flow, preserve critical habitats, and promote the adoption of sustainable land use practices.

description:
This is the area covered by marine forests mainly mangrove. It is located in Pangani Districts and covers Thirteen coast villages. Within this area, there are human settlements (villages) and tourist hotels. According to the Tanzania Forest Service TFS Pangani office, the exact mangrove area is about 3750 Hectares. 

In this project, the ambakofi organization will work with the small-scale fishing community to conserve the existing and restore the degraded mangrove site.  ambakofi will conduct community-based Ecological Mangrove Restoration (CBEMR) training to build capacity for the villagers living adjacent to mangrove forests.  

Due to the high destruction of the mangrove forest due to the need for building materials, wood fuel, animal grazing, and climate effects, there is a high need to conserve the remaining mangroves. But at the same time, we highly need to restore all the sites facing huge degradation from human and non-anthropogenic causes.

All over the world, the common restoration action applied is planting of the mangrove. This has proved to be a failure in many projects related to mangrove restoration. Due to its nature and different biological factors, most of the planted mangroves ended up drying and died a few days after planting activity. Very few seedlings can survive but it stands as a loss compared to the number of planted seedlings/saplings. Because planting is not an assurance way of restoring mangroves, ambakofi comes with a CBEMR approach which shows positive signs of achievements. 

However since the main target implementors of CBEMR techniques do not know how to implement this natural regeneration way, we need to train them theoretically and practically so they become true custodians of this valuable resource to nature and humanity.

In CBEMR selected participants will be trained in the easy and understandable ways of conducting restoration naturally. The training model will include; step-by-step techniques for planning a mangrove restoration project. This includes Conducting social, environmental and economic research, identifying mangrove species found in the target area, identifying any changes happening in the area and what causes those changes, brainstorming and discussing the goal of the restoration, and implementation, especially in hydrological cycle, mangrove ecology and biology, stress management, identifying mangrove enemies, monitoring and evaluation and only plant if the available seeds/seedlings can sprout and grow. Other aspects of CBEMR are mangrove zoning, measuring salinity level and soil pH.  

CBEMR training is already conducted in four villages among 13 available villages on the coast of Pangani District. Trained villages are Ushongo, Stahabu, Kipumbwi and Sange

description: The Western Tanzania is home to globally unique but highly endangered vegetation . Over 20% of around 9000 plant species are now threatened with extinction.The lack of awareness of the importance of maintaining biodiversity on agricultural land in the region as well as lacking decision-making power of women and the inadequate enforcement of biodiversity laws lead to an intensification of the problem. Rising eastward , the KIU forest encompasses over 800ha of mostly forested landscape. This ecosystem is home to approximately 93 percent of Tanzania’s 2,800 endangered chimpanzees . Although they support important biodiversity and provide local and regional ecosystem services, the biodiversity areas within western Tanzania have limited legal protection and are under increasing pressure from expansion of permanent croplands, unsustainable resource use, habitat fragmentation and charcoal burning. These challenges are compounded by the lack of voice and participation in decision-making by local communities, and risks of land expropriation to external parties.

name: Kafue National Park
description:
Kafue National Park, covering an expansive 22,400 km2 in western Zambia, makes up a significant portion of the world’s largest transboundary conservation area, known as the Kavango-Zambezi Transfrontier Conservation Area (KAZA TFCA). The park was proclaimed in 1950, making it Zambia’s oldest national park and one of the world’s most important natural heritage sites. As an essential water source for the region, Kafue is also one of the last vast expanses of the iconic Zambezian ecoregion – and home to elephant, large predators, the highest diversity of antelope species in Africa, and 515 bird species.

Lack of funding and effective management over the years hampered park operations and allowed poaching, human encroachment and charcoal production to take their toll on both landscape and wildlife. Yet large tracts of wilderness containing a diversity of wildlife species still remain intact. In 2021, Zambia’s Department of National Parks and Wildlife (DNPW) invited African Parks to implement a Priority Support Plan. Over 18 months, significant infrastructure investments were made, protection measures improved, over 200 jobs created, and education enhanced through a literacy programme. This paved the way for a 20-year management agreement between African Parks and the Zambian government in July 2022, for the full protection of Kafue’s valuable landscape.

Kafue’s expansive landscape, its variety of lodges and the recovering wildlife is an opportunity to boost Zambia’s tourism industry and deliver critically needed revenue for the park, and provide employment and benefits to local communities. In this way, Kafue can fulfil its promise to become one of Africa’s most exceptional tourist destinations.

name: Bangweulu Wetland
description:
Located in north-eastern Zambia, Bangweulu Wetland’s rich and diverse ecosystem forms one of Africa’s most important wetlands. This community-owned protected area is not just a life source for wildlife, such as endemic black lechwe and hundreds of bird species, but also for the 60,000 people who live there. Bangweulu is unique in that it is made up of Game Management Areas (GMAs), where community members have retained the right to sustainably harvest natural resources. Following unsustainable pressure on Bangweulu’s wildlife and fish stocks, in 2008, six Community Resource Boards (CRBs) and the Department of National Parks and Wildlife (DNPW) entered into a long-term agreement with African Parks to deliver on a shared vision to sustainably manage and protect these natural assets long into the future.

Since then, many advances have taken place: poaching has been largely contained, resulting in the recovery of fish stocks, and allowing a dramatic increase in the black lechwe and tsessebe populations, and the historic return of the African cheetah. In addition to creating a more sustainable landscape and providing food security for local residents, the collaboration between government, communities and African Parks has resulted in the construction and funding of schools and the creation of a mobile health outreach programme.

There is much work to be done to ensure that Bangweulu continues to provide for the coming generations, but through effective management and strong community engagement, people are now taking part in and planning for their future, recognising their livelihoods are linked to a thriving wetland.

name: Liuwa Plain National Park
description:
Liuwa Plain in western Zambia has one of the longest conservation histories in Africa, dating back to the late 19th century when the King of Barotseland appointed his people as the custodians of the reserve.

Liuwa Plain National Park in Zambia has one of the longest conservation histories in Africa, dating back to the 19th century when the King of Barotseland, Lubosi Lewanika, appointed his people as custodians of the landscape. But, by the turn of this century, decades of unsustainable land-use, poaching and human-wildlife conflict had caused a large decline in species such as wildebeest and zebra, allowed agriculture to threaten the grasslands, and reduced the lion population to just one lonely lioness, “Lady Liuwa”. In 2003, realising what was at stake, the Department of National Parks and Wildlife (DNPW) and the Barotse Royal Establishment (BRE) invited African Parks to help restore the legacy of Liuwa Plain. As a result of effective conservation law enforcement, poaching decreased and community land-use plans were implemented along with sustainable fish harvesting and other community projects, providing alternative livelihoods for local people. In 2008, African Parks began a series of lion reintroductions, and a new life began for Lady Liuwa as she joined a pride. Over a similar period, eland and buffalo were reintroduced to the park and plains game began to increase, providing a healthy prey base for the predators: lion, cheetah and hyaena.

Today, with over 10,000 people legally living within the park, Liuwa is a prime example of how people and wildlife can coexist and benefit in a shared landscape. Helping protect the land for the benefit of local people to continue accessing its natural resources sustainably is enhanced through ongoing community engagement and integration. In addition, communities are supported through socio-economic initiatives, employment and tourism revenue that is generated as Liuwa becomes a major tourist attraction. Now that the landscape is once again a source of stability and abundance, the people of Liuwa have renewed their commitment and sense of custodianship to their land.

name: Kabwafu Agroforestry Project
description: The primary land use patterns in the project area are those of the rural sector characterised by small-scale farmers in pursuit of their livelihoods. This has resulted in a landscape mosaic of rural dwellings and arable fields within the background matrix of Miombo woodland and dambos, which have been opened to a greater or lesser extent. The project area comprises a landscape mosaic of rural dwellings, tobacco barns, cultivated crops, gum plantations and Miombo woodland remnants. Around the homesteads, the staple foods maize and cassava are intercropped on a small scale with groundnuts, vegetables and fruit trees. Livestock in the project area is mainly for subsistence purposes. Tobacco is a cash crop, and growers are one of several land users to open up Miombo woodlands.

name: Liwonde National Park
description:
Since 2015, Liwonde National Park has been the site of some significant wildlife translocations and reintroductions, transforming it into a sanctuary for Malawi’s wildlife. When African Parks assumed management of Liwonde, in partnership with the Department of National Parks and Wildlife (DNPW) in 2015, the park was riddled with tens of thousands of wire snares – more snares existed than large animals – and it had some of the highest human-wildlife conflict levels in the region.

But since then, Liwonde has established one of the most effective conservation law enforcement measures and training in southern Africa, integrated advanced technology to protect and monitor wildlife, removed more than 40,000 wire snares, and orchestrated a number of historic animal reintroductions.

In 2017, African Parks began re-establishing Liwonde’s predator population by bringing back cheetah, which had been absent from the park for a century. This was followed in 2018 by a founder population of lion, and wild dog in 2021. In 2019, 17 black rhino were relocated from South Africa to Liwonde, in one of the largest international black rhino translocations in history.

With wildlife populations on the rise, as well as the number of people who visit the park to witness its revival, Liwonde National Park has been restored, transforming it into a safe haven to benefit both the wildlife and the people who live here.

name: Mkupe Conservation
description:
The mangroves of Mkupe Creek are unique because of their peri-urban setting so close to the settlements of Miritini, Changamwe and Mombasa’s Old Town. As you are wandering through the tree line, you will spot the high rises of Mombasa in the distance. This sets the project apart from other mangrove restoration projects in Kenya, which happen in settings that are more ‘conventional’.

The other thing that makes this site unique is the manner in which the restoration work is deeply entwined with the local community around there, and how they are willing to participate in restoration projects. The climate in Mkupe is also favorable, as it experiences a hot and humid tropical climate with temperatures ranging between 24°C and 30°C, and mean annual rainfall range between 1000 and 1600 mm/yr.

name: Gitovu Hill, Bubanza
description:
Many of Burundi’s lower mountain forests, also known as the East African montane forests, have been stripped of their needle-leaved and evergreen species. 

The use of improper agricultural planes and terraces, the overharvesting of tree products and the growing need for firewood have caused a decline in soil fertility. Steep slopes and frequent rainfall exacerbate the problem of the leaching of soils; the removal of water-soluble nutrients from the ground. 

We plant trees in Nyagonga. Many seedlings here are planted in biodegradable bags made from banana peels in order to establish plastic-free tree nurseries. Such practices are taught to the local community and in schools in order for the local community to become successful stewards of the forests in the future.

name: Iringa CDI3
description:
Trees for the Future (TREES) has planted more than 250 million trees since it was founded in 1989.

In addition to enhancing ecological and environmental benefits at planting sites around the world, TREES’ staff are experts in agroforestry, which combines agriculture and forestry to create integrated and sustainable land-use systems. TREES aim to address the problem of degraded and over-worked lands by providing farmers with tree seeds, technical training, onsite planning and assistance, and an overall reclamation and business plan for their future.

TREES works with the Clinton Development Initiative (CDI) to train and equip local farmers within the Community Agri-Business program to plant trees consisting of agroforestry, fruit trees, and timber trees to improve agriculture sustainability and livelihoods development. This involves delivering appropriate, effective tree-planting support through training, extension of a loan package that includes trees and vegetable seeds, tree sacs and a few tools to help farmers to plant trees within specific target communities.

name: The Ellen DeGeneres Campus of the Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund
description:
The multi-acre, eco-friendly facility adjacent to the Volcanoes National Park includes three main buildings – the Sandy and Harold Price Research Center, the Rob and Melani Walton Education Center and the Cindy Broder Conservation Gallery – as well as housing for visiting students and researchers. The Ellen Campus is designed to serve as a gateway to conservation for the many stakeholders with whom we work as well as visitors from around the world, helping to create the next generation of conservationists.

Science is at the core of what we do at the Fossey Fund. The Sandy and Harold Price Research Center is a state-of-the-art facility aimed at advancing our research in areas like genetics, physiology and paleontology. The five-fold increase in lab space as compared to our prior facility provides new opportunities to work with scientific collaborators and students as well as more training opportunities for young African conservationists.

"The Ellen Campus represents a huge expansion of our teaching and laboratory spaces, enabling us to not just increase but transform our programs to study gorillas and their critical forest habitat and bring educational opportunities to early career African scientists and members of the local community." Felix Ndagijimana, director of Rwanda programs, Dian Fossey Gorilla Fund

Central to our mission is education. Expanded classroom space, combined with a science library and computer lab, enhance our teaching opportunities with local and international universities and enable us to host conferences, seminars and trainings. But the educational opportunities extend beyond the classroom – indeed, the whole Ellen Campus serves as an educational tool. For example, the campus is literally a living laboratory – the more than 250,000 native plants that make up the Cleveland Metroparks Zoo Interpretive Trails provide a rich experience for field trips. In addition, the Cindy Broder Conservation Gallery contains an immersive public exhibit designed to tell the story of mountain gorilla research and conservation from Dian’s time to the present day. It includes original, never-before-seen artifacts from Dian Fossey’s nearly two decades living with the gorillas, stunning visual experiences, including virtual and augmented reality and a 360-degree immersive theater, and numerous engaging edu-tainment opportunities to learn more about the science and the people behind the conservation success of mountain gorillas.

name: Forests for Life 3: Mulanje A1
description:
The Mlatho Hills Catchment Project was initiated in partnership with the Mulanje Mission Hospital . Mulanje Mission Hospital, through its Sustainable Livelihoods programme, aims to promote and support activities which underpin a broad approach to improving community health and nutrition. One such area is agricultural development, and the sustainable livelihoods approach - poverty reduction, reducing livelihood vulnerability, improving environmental sustainability through participatory approaches, are key aspects of the work carried out by MMH since the foundation of the programme in 2017. 

the main objective of this project is to reduce poverty by strengthening the skills, competencies, abilities and resources of communities and to create an enabling environment for accessing income-generating opportunities to address basic needs, thereby improving socioeconomic well-being. In particular, this project focuses on reforesting 2 hectares of indigenous forest, training communities in sustainable forest management, expanding the implementation of agroforestry, increasing the use of improved cookstove technology, and developing income-generating tree and forest product enterprises such as beekeeping. 

Year Planted: 2020
Trees planted: 2500
Hectares restored: 3.63 ha

For more information on our work, visit:
https://www.greenpop.org

description:
The site is located in the Mau Region of southern Kenya. Between 1990 and 2015, 311,000 hectares of forest were lost in Kenya, and in 2019 the government set a target of increasing tree cover by 10% by 2022. Restoring forests will support local biodiversity - providing shelter, shade and food for many species. Planting native trees allows areas to naturally regenerate, encouraging plants and animals to return to areas where they used to live.

A wide variety of native species will be planted in this site, including trees that will provide new food sources for local people, including avocado, lemon and papaya trees. 
Seeds are sourced locally from nearby existing forests, and prepared for planting in the nurseries by forming small seed balls, which are a mixture of soil, compost and seeds. The seed balls can be made in the dry season in preparation for planting in the rainy season The seeds are germinated and nurtured in the local nurseries to ensure high germination rates and to raise strong, healthy seedlings.

Over the course of the project, more than 14, million native species Afromontane trees will be planted at the site.

name: East Usambara FLR Project
description:
The East Usambara Forest Landscape Restoration Project (EUFLR), is a five-year initiative (2022-
2026) sponsored by WWF-Switzerland (WWF-CH), it aims to restore and protect East Usambara
sub-montane, lowland, and coastal forests for the local community's livelihoods and wildlife.
The project is implemented in two districts in Tanga Region i.e., Mkinga DC (six villages) and
Korogwe DC (Six villages). The project's ultimate goal is for forests, wetlands, and their essential
species in the East Usambara sub-montane, lowland, and coastal forests to be sustainably
protected and contribute to increased ecological services and peoples' livelihoods by 2026. This
goal will be accomplished using a variety of tactics, including 1) awareness raising/mobilization
and capacity building of Local Governments, Communities, Village CBOs, and CSOs on Natural
resources policies and advocacy, 2) Forest Restoration to ensure wildlife habitat connectivity, 3)
promoting sustainable energy technologies, 4) spatial planning, and 5) promoting sustainable
Climate Smart Agriculture (CSA).
To date, project team has completed number of activities including; Village land use planning in
six project villages, support Human Elephant Conflict (HEC), establishment of tree nurseries,
and piloting of Farmer Field Business schools to facilitate CSA practices and market linkages.

Maasai Mara University is the only Institution of learning serving historically marginalized regions in the South Rift including Kajiado and Narok Counties and the densely populated Counties of Bomet and Kericho. It currently offers a total of fifty-two (52) Undergraduate, fifty (50) Postgraduate Nine (9) Diploma and six (6) Certificate programmes. The University is however scaling down the Academic Programmes to retain only those that respond to the University’s overall niche and are able to attract students. So far out of the fifty-two (52) the University has discontinued fifteen (15) academic programmes and is continuing to re-engineer the remaining and merging others. The University has continued to review and develop market driven programmes in response to existing and emerging concerns as well as train students who are able to create employment.  The University’s strategic location within the greater Mara-Mau Ecosystem places it in the forefront in addressing challenges within the region as well as contribute to the national development agenda. Some of the local challenges the University is addressing through its academic and research activities are indicated below: 
a)	Deforestation: The University is located next to the Mau forest complex, a key water catchment area with high level of deforestation arising from encroachment of the forest land.   The University offers a Bachelor of Science in Forestry Ecosystems Management and is involved in research and outreach activities aimed at restoration of the Mau forest complex as well as engaging the local community on the negative effects of environmental degrading activities such as charcoal burning. The National Museums and Monuments of Zimbabwe (NMMZ) says it is working on modalities to declare Nerumedzo forests a national heritage site.
A locally known and accepted myth is that the forest is the home of the spirit of Nerumedzo, an ancestor who escaped death from his father because he was born with four eyes. The spirit of the legendary Nemeso is believed to still dwell in the forest and is responsible for the seasonal migration of the stink bug (harurwa) which in time has come to be seen as ancestral “manna from heaven” Harurwa remains one of the most unexpectedly sought after edible insects in Southern Africa.

name: Kuruwitu Tengefu
description:
KCW CBO was set up in 2003 by members of the community who were concerned about the degradation of their seas. Over fishing, climate change and uncontrolled fish and coral collection by the aquarium trade needed to be addressed before the marine ecosystem was damaged beyond repair.

Elders who could remember how healthy and productive the sea had been decades ago told their story and KCW – CBO put together a management plan for sustainable fisheries alongside other alternative income generating enterprises. In 2005 they took the unprecedented step of setting aside a 30 hectare Marine Protected Area (MPA). This was the first coral based Locally Managed Marine Area (LMMA) in Kenya. 12 years on, the area has made a remarkable recovery.

With fishing prohibited within the MPA, fish have grown in abundance, size and diversity. The area has become a breeding ground, leading to an increase in fish outside the MPA. As such, fishermen see greater catches due to a spillover effect. At the same time, biodiversity has increased dramatically making Kuruwitu a destination for eco-tourism creating jobs for guides, boat captains and rangers.

KCW – CBO is working with the local Beach Management Unit (BMU), the Kenyan State Department of Fisheries, the Wildlife Conservation Society (WCS) and Oceans Alive to develop a co-management plan that will cover a 12 square kilometer area of ocean off the Kenyan coast. Through plan, KCWO will work with local fishermen to promote the sustainable use of marine resources, to reduce post-harvest losses and improve fish marketing systems.

name: Kuruwitu Co-Management Area
description:
The Kuruwitu Co-Management Area has come into force to complement community efforts in conservation and management of fisheries and marine resources by managing the resources in collaboration with the government.
Our pilot Kuruwitu BMU (KBMU) has been assisted to develop the first official CO-Management Area (CMA). The 12000 ha site caters for 500 members and over 10,000 fishery value chain livelihoods. The BMU has been supported to strengthen its institutional by laws and policing of the CMA.

name: Lake Jipe Ecosystem
description:
Lake Jipe is a unique transboundary freshwater ecosystem located on the border of Kenya and Tanzania. Here's a description of the Lake Jipe ecosystem:

1. Geography and Location:
   - Lake Jipe is situated in East Africa, straddling the border between Kenya and Tanzania.
   - It is part of the Great Rift Valley, a region known for its geological and ecological significance.
   - The lake covers an area of approximately 28 square kilometers, making it relatively small in size.

2. Hydrology:
   - Lake Jipe is primarily fed by the waters of the Lumi River, which flows from the north. This river is crucial for the lake's water inflow.
   - The lake is also affected by the Ruvu River, which serves as its outlet, draining the water from Lake Jipe into the Indian Ocean.
   - The lake is relatively shallow, with an average depth of about 3 meters, and it can experience significant fluctuations in water levels.

3. Biodiversity:
   - Lake Jipe is known for its rich biodiversity. The lake and its surrounding areas are home to a variety of plant and animal species.
   - The lake supports various fish species, including tilapia and catfish, which are essential for local fisheries.
   - The surrounding wetlands and marshes provide habitats for numerous bird species, making it an important area for birdwatching.

4. Wetlands and Vegetation:
   - The lake is surrounded by wetlands and papyrus reed beds, which serve as critical habitats for various species, including birds and fish.
   - The vegetation in the area includes papyrus reeds, water lilies, and other aquatic plants.

5. Wildlife:
   - The Lake Jipe ecosystem is home to a variety of wildlife, including elephants, hippos, crocodiles, and numerous bird species.
   - The presence of elephants in the region is a unique aspect of the ecosystem, as they move through the area in search of resources like water and food.

6. Human Activities:
   - The lake and its surrounding areas support various human activities, including fishing, crop farming, and livestock husbandry.
   - Local communities depend on the lake for their livelihoods, and they have traditionally coexisted with the wildlife in the area.
   - However, human-wildlife conflicts, particularly with elephants, have become a significant concern in recent years.

7. Threats:
   - The Lake Jipe ecosystem faces several threats, including overfishing, siltation, soil erosion, and invasive species.
   - Climate change impacts, including changes in rainfall patterns, have also affected the ecosystem.
   - Pollution, driven by agricultural practices and waste disposal, is a growing concern in the area.

In summary, Lake Jipe is a small but ecologically diverse freshwater ecosystem in East Africa. It supports a range of wildlife, including elephants and various bird species, making it a unique and valuable natural resource. However, it faces challenges related to human activities and environmental changes that require conservation efforts to protect its ecological integrity.

name: Lake Ol'Bolossat
description:
Karbonisierung von Biomasse  – ein neuer Ansatz zur Ernährungssicherheit, Wohlstand und Naturschutz für eine marginalisierte Gruppe am Lake Ol’Bolossat (Kenia) 

Im Dorf Bahati in Kenia leben über 300 Menschen auf nur ca. 4,2 Hektar. Es sind Turkana, die in den 1960er Jahren als Arbeiter an den Lake Ol’Bolossat kamen. Sie sind arm, arbeitslos und haben keine höhere Bildung. Konflikte um begrenzt verfügbare Ressourcen sauberes Wasser, Lebensmittel, etc. wurden immer größer. Wilderei an den Grauen Kronenkranichen war an der Tagesordnung, die Eier und auch die Tiere selbst dienten als Nahrung und/oder wurden verkauft. Zum Schutz der Grauen Kronenkraniche wurde 2015 die Cranes Conservation Volunteers gegründet. Durch viel  Aufklärungsarbeit konnten die Dorfbewohner von der Wilderei abgebracht werden.
Das größere Problem für die Vögel ist jedoch nicht der Mensch, sondern der Wasserfarn (Salvinia molesta), ein invasives Wasserunkraut aus der Amazonasregion. Er breitet sich über das Gefieder von Wasservögeln sehr großflächig  im See und in den Feuchtgebieten dieses Ökosystems aus. In den nährstoffhaltigen Gewässern Afrikas wächst Salvinia explosionsartig und erstickt jede andere Vegetation, so z.B. das Schilf, das den Grauen Kranichen und anderen Vögeln als Rückzug dienen soll. An vielen Stellen des Sees gibt es jedoch nur noch offenes Wasser, das komplett von Salvinia bedeckt ist, dort finden die Tiere keinen Schutz. Salvinia ist ein Klimakiller. Wenn es abstirbt, sinkt es auf den Gewässerboden und wird dort von Bakterien zersetzt. Dabei entsteht Biogas, eine Mischung aus Methan (CH4) und Kohlendioxid (CO2), welches im Gewässer aufsteigt und sich mit der Luft verbindet. So gelangen Unmengen von Methan in die Atmosphäre, mit verheerendem Effekt auf unser Klima. Salvinia gehört zu den größten natürlichen Emittenten von Methan und birgt somit ein unglaubliches Klimaschutzpotential. Pro Tonne Salvinia-Pflanzenkohle kann Methan in Höhe von 393 Tonnen CO2-Äquivalente vermieden werden. Anfang 2021 wurde begonnen, Salvinia aus dem See zu fischen, zu trocknen und zu karbonisieren. Die Salvinia-Kohle wurde mit Ziegendung gemischt und in die Erde ausgebracht. Die Wachstumserfolge bei verschiedenen Gemüsesorten waren enorm. Salvinia ist Biomasse, aus der auch Kompost hergestellt werden kann, dem Salvinia-Kohle beigegeben wird, um die Qualität zu steigern. Dieser Dünger kommt direkt in den Boden. Der Dünger kann auf dem Markt zu einem günstigeren Preis als der traditionelle Tierdungmist, der zudem lange Transportwege hat, angeboten werden. So entstehen Arbeitsplätze für die Turkana.
Projektziele: Klimaschutz durch Vermeidung von Methan. Die Turkana führen ein selbstbestimmtes Leben und können ihre Familien selbstständig und eigenverantwortlich versorgen. Die traditionellen Anbaumethoden werden verfeinert. Der See wird kontinuierlich von Salvinia befreit. Mit Salvinia-Kohle kann der ertragsschwache, saure Boden in einem Schritt für mehr als 100 Jahre fruchtbar gemacht werden.  Durch die Nutzung von Salvinia wird dessen Ausbreitung verlangsamt, das Schilf kann sich wieder etablieren. Entwicklung von Ökotourismus
